chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:

I said to him, 'I manumitted a slave-girl for some orphans of ours, and stipulated upon her that if she became unable (to pay), she would return to slavery, and I would be free of what I had taken from her.' He said, 'Your stipulation is valid.' And it will be said to you, 'Indeed, Ali (peace be upon him) used to say: The manumitted slave is freed proportionate to what he pays of his manumission contract.' I said, 'That was only Ali's (peace be upon him) opinion before the stipulation was made; when people made stipulations, they had their own stipulation.' I said to him, 'What is the definition of inability (ajz)?' He said, 'Indeed, our judges say that the inability of the manumitted slave is that he delays the installment (najm) to the next installment until a year passes over him.' I said, 'What do you say?' He said, 'No, and no concession: he does not have the right to delay an installment beyond its due time if that is part of his stipulation.'

key_terms.النَّجْم: An installment or period in a manumission contract
key_terms.شَرْط: Stipulation or condition agreed upon in a contract
key_terms.عَجْز: Inability or incapacity to fulfill an obligation
key_terms.مُكَاتَب: A slave who has entered into a contract to pay a sum of money to his master in exchange for freedom

ai.seo_question: What is the legal definition of inability (ajz) for a mukatab slave and how does a specific stipulation affect manumission?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfabar illustrates the Shia juristic principle of 'al-shartu lahum ma shartu' (the stipulation is for them as they stipulated), where contractual freedom overrides the general prophetic precedent of Ali (AS) regarding proportional manumission. It establishes a critical legal distinction between 'inability' (ajz) defined by a full year's delay in standard contexts versus immediate default upon missing a specific due date when such a condition is explicitly agreed upon. This reflects the pragmatic application of contract law in early Islamic society, balancing the protection of the slave's path to freedom with the creditor's rights.
